note: Vol. I No. 14. The issue that puts a documented storefront off South Water Street for the first time — J. K. Botsford's tin shop at the corner of Dearborn and Lake — and that says where the town's shingles and lath came from: across the lake from Michigan in the Schooner Post Boy, as soon as the ice cleared. The Chicago Academy's second term, its two departments and its board of trustees close the month.

claims.notes: A SECOND DOCUMENTED CORNER, AND IT IS NOT ON SOUTH WATER STREET. Every placed storefront this month has sat on South Water; J. K. Botsford's tin shop is at the CORNER OF DEARBORN AND LAKE STREETS, which puts a documented business one block north of the river frontage and is the first Lake Street address the epic has. It also resolves the previous week's relative address: Botsford was 'next door to Graves' Tavern' on 17 February (1834-02-18, claim c004), so Graves' Tavern is next door to the Dearborn and Lake corner — an inference stated in both notes and written into neither placement, because the tavern has no claim of its own. THE TRADE IS A MANUFACTURE, NOT ONLY A STOCK: he sells tin ware brought express from Detroit now and will MAKE tin 'in all its branches' when navigation opens, which dates a workshop to the spring of 1834 and is a good example of how completely the lake's ice governed the town's year.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S SCHOOL, ITS TERM DATES, ITS FUNDING AND ITS BOARD. The Chicago Academy's SECOND term began on Monday 17 February 1834 — the notice says 'the 15th inst.', which was the Saturday, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than corrected — and it has just been placed under the public funds for schools, which is a real change of status and not a puff: a subscription academy becoming a publicly funded one inside its first year. It has TWO DEPARTMENTS and it owns charts, maps and globes, which is the closest thing to an inventory of a Chicago schoolroom's contents the epic has found. The board is named: J. Snow, [J.] D. Graves and G. T. Sproat. GRAVES IS THE NAME TO NOTICE — Botsford's shop is 'next door to Graves' Tavern' (1834-02-18, claim c004), and a D. Graves sitting on the school board is very likely the same man, which is stated and not merged: the gazetteer keys on the whole name and 'D. Graves' and 'Graves' stay two entries until a witness joins them. Sproat is the G. N. Sproat who wrote the Presbyterian dedication hymn in January, or his relative; same refusal applies. NO SCHOOLHOUSE IS NAMED OR PLACED and none is supplied — the institution is documented, the building is not.

business.name: a storage, commission and lumber business, proprietor unnamed in the cited range

claims.notes: WHERE THE TOWN'S BUILDING MATERIALS CAME FROM, IN THE MERCHANT'S OWN WORDS. Lath, shingles, red cedar posts and 'all articles in the lumber line' — the finish materials, not the framing — shipped ACROSS THE LAKE from Michigan and unloadable only 'as soon as the ice is clear', with a named vessel chartered for the first two trips: the Schooner Post Boy. This is the supply side of the building-materials prices the Democrat quotes weekly (1834-02-04, claim c011), and together they say something a reconstruction has to honour: a Chicago building of 1834-35 is roofed with shingles that crossed Lake Michigan in a schooner after the ice went out. The man also keeps a STORE — flour, grain and country produce — so this is a lumber yard and a provision store in one hand. HIS NAME IS NOT IN THE CITED RANGE: the notice's signature falls below the column's foot and is not supplied, so the business is recorded without a proprietor rather than being attributed to the Calvin Britain named as his agent at St. Joseph. That refusal is the claim's honesty and not an oversight — a firm named wrongly is worse than a firm unnamed.

The reading here is worse than the 18 February printing (1834-02-18, claim c007) and the quantities are supplied from it rather than guessed.

claims.notes: THE LIVERY STABLE'S SECOND PRINTING, AND IT CARRIES THE DATELINE THE FIRST ONE DID NOT: Chicago, 11 February 1834. So the stable at the Point opened in the second week of February 1834 and was still advertising a fortnight later — a dated start for a building, which is what the reconstruction needs and what a standing advertisement usually withholds. The proprietors' line is cut here and is supplied from the 18 February printing (claim c003 there), where it reads whole.
